notes.meaning: After taking control of Babylon, King Darius set up a new system of government over his kingdom. He appointed one hundred and twenty regional leaders called satraps to govern the provinces, and he placed three top administrators over them, including Daniel. These three overseers audited the governors so the king would not be cheated out of taxes or face rebellions.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many historians question the existence of Darius the Mede because secular Persian records do not mention a monarch by that name between the Babylonian fall and Cyrus the Great.

notes.meaning: Daniel quickly stood out above all the other leaders because of his remarkable spirit, clear wisdom, and deep honesty. Even though he was an elderly Jewish exile, King Darius trusted him so much that he planned to place him in charge of the entire empire. This planned promotion stirred up intense jealousy among the other high officials.

The jealous leaders closely inspected Daniel's public life and record, hoping to uncover fraud, neglect, or treason. They found nothing to criticize because he was completely trustworthy and worked with clean hands. Realizing they could not attack his professional record, they concluded they could only trap him through his obedience to God's law.

The officials gathered as a group and approached the king, using smooth speech to hide their wicked scheme. They falsely claimed that all the governors had agreed on a new law, even though Daniel was never consulted. They asked the king to decree that for thirty days, no one could pray or make any request to any god or man except to Darius himself, with violators thrown into the lions' den.

The men urged the king to sign the written order immediately to make it unbreakable under the legal system of the Medes and Persians. In their culture, once a royal decree was written and sealed, not even the king himself could repeal it. Flattered by the idea of being treated as supreme, Darius signed the document without realizing the trap.

As soon as Daniel learned that the decree had been signed into law, he went straight to his house to pray. He opened the upper windows facing toward Jerusalem, the ruined city where God had placed His temple, and knelt down three times that day to give thanks and plead with God. He made no effort to hide his worship, maintaining the exact pattern of prayer he had practiced all his life.

The plotting officials gathered and rushed to Daniel's home, where they caught him in the act of praying and asking God for help. They hurried to the palace and reminded the king about his strict thirty-day ban, making sure he confirmed that the law could not be changed.

Once the king confirmed the law was unchangeable, the men brought their charge against Daniel. They spoke of him with contempt, calling him merely an exile from Judah rather than a top minister, and claimed he showed complete disrespect toward the king and his royal decree by continuing to pray three times a day.

Hearing Daniel's name crushed the king, and he was furious with himself for falling into such a foolish trap. Darius spent the rest of the day looking for any legal loophole to save his faithful minister until the sun went down. The conspirators returned in a crowd at sunset to remind the king that Medo-Persian law strictly forbade altering any royal statute.

Feeling completely helpless before his own law, the king gave the order, and Daniel was thrown into the pit of wild lions. Before leaving him, Darius expressed a desperate hope that Daniel's God, whom he served so faithfully, would rescue him. A large stone was rolled over the entrance, and the king and his nobles stamped their signet rings in wax on it so no one could open the pit secretly.

Darius returned to his palace in deep sorrow and spent the entire night without eating. He refused to listen to music or enjoy any customary palace entertainment, and his guilt kept him from sleeping a wink. His sleepless distress shows how deeply he regretted his prideful decision.

At the very first sign of dawn, the king got up and rushed to the lions' den. Drawing near, he cried out in a voice broken with grief, asking whether the living God, whom Daniel served without ceasing, had been able to save him from the wild beasts.

Daniel answered from within the pit with standard court respect, wishing the king long life. He announced that God had sent His angel to shut the lions' mouths so they could not harm him. The Lord protected him because he was innocent before heaven, and Daniel had committed no crime against the king by remaining faithful to God.

The king was filled with overwhelming relief and ordered Daniel to be pulled up out of the pit immediately. When they examined him, he had not suffered a single scratch or bite. Daniel was preserved not by luck or human skill, but because he placed complete trust in his God.

Darius then ordered the arrest of the men who had plotted Daniel's death, along with their wives and children, and had them thrown into the same pit. Under ancient Persian customs, entire households were held responsible for treason. The lions attacked them ferociously, crushing their bones before they even touched the pit floor, proving the animals had not spared Daniel out of a lack of hunger.

King Darius then sent a public letter to all the different peoples and languages throughout his vast empire. He commanded everyone to show deep reverence before the God of Daniel, describing Him as the living, eternal Lord whose kingdom will never fall. Unlike worthless idols, Daniel's God works real signs and wonders across heaven and earth, as shown by His miraculous deliverance from the lions.

Daniel continued to thrive in high office during the remainder of Darius's reign and into the rule of Cyrus the Persian. God honored His faithful servant with long life, honor, and influence across multiple rulers and empires. Standing firm in private devotion brought divine blessing on his public service.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read the phrase 'reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus' as referring to a single person, meaning 'the reign of Darius, that is, the reign of Cyrus.'
